title: Hello, World! Tutorial
blurb: Never written code before? Start here. Boss a robot around, then take tiny steps from your first line to your first function.
intro:
Welcome! This tutorial is for you if you have never written a line of code. Stage 1 has no code at all: you give a very literal robot its orders, which is exactly what programming is. Every stage is tiny: read a few sentences, type a line or two, press RUN, and see what happens.

You'll print messages, store things in variables, do a bit of math, make a choice with if, repeat with a loop, and write your very first function. Mistakes are completely fine. The game reads your code and tells you what went wrong in plain words.

Tip

When you finish here, head to the Main Path and start with Variables. Everything you see in this tutorial gets a full section there.

stages.hook: A hungry robot wants a jam sandwich, and you're in charge. The catch: it does exactly what you say. Nothing more, nothing less.
stages.l:
Before you write any code, here's the biggest secret in programming: computers do exactly what you tell them, in the order you tell them. They never guess what you meant.

Code is just a list of very precise orders. Let's practise being precise with no code at all.
stages.p:
Tap the orders so the robot makes a jam sandwich, then press GO, ROBOT.

Any order that makes sense works. In a real kitchen you could open the jar first or grab the bread first, and so can the robot. It only stops when you ask for something it can't do yet.

Watch out: two of the orders are too vague. A person would know what you mean, but a robot needs every small step spelled out. Leave those two out. Not sure which ones? Add one, press GO, and see what the robot does with it.
stages.h:
The two vague orders each squash several small steps into one. Spot them and leave them out.

For the rest, ask of every order: what does the robot need before it can do this? Dipping the knife needs an open jar and a knife in hand. Spreading needs jam on the knife and bread on the plate.
stages.s:
Pick up two slices of bread
Lay them flat on the plate
Unscrew the lid of the jam jar
Pick up the knife
Dip the knife in the jar
Spread the jam on one slice
Put the other slice on top
done: Two slices of bread, picked up.
Both slices lie flat on the plate.
The lid comes off with a pop.
The knife comes out covered in jam.
One slice is now nicely jammy.
Sandwich complete! The robot beeps happily.

vague.lit: The robot freezes. Make it how? It has no idea what the steps of a sandwich are.
vague.why: This order is too vague: it hides every step at once. Take it out and use the small, exact orders instead.

vague.lit: The robot scoops jam out with its bare metal hand and slaps it on. You never said to use a knife!
vague.why: Too vague: it skips opening the jar, picking up the knife and dipping it. The exact orders already cover all of that, so take this one out.

stages.early: The robot tries, but it can't do that yet. Something else has to happen first.
need: Lay what flat? The robot isn't holding any bread yet.
Clunk! The knife bangs against the lid. The jar is still closed.
Dip what? The robot's hand is empty. It needs to pick up the knife first.
Spread it where? There's no bread on the plate yet.
The robot spreads... nothing. There's no jam on the knife yet.
Put it on top of what? There's no jammy slice to cover yet.
stages.okMsg: The robot only cares that each step is possible when you ask for it. Opening the jar first, or grabbing the knife before the bread, works just as well. Code is the same: often several orders work, as long as nothing is used before it's ready.

stages.l:
Hi @@name, welcome to coding! Programmers have a tradition: the very first program anyone writes just says hello.

console.log() prints whatever you put between the brackets. Text goes inside quotes.

console.log("Hi there!");
Hi there!

Now write your own line that prints Hello, world! instead, then press RUN. Capital letters, the comma and the quotes all matter.
stages.h: Use the same shape as the example, but put Hello, world! between the quotes.
stages.st: // Type your first line of code below
stages.altNote: Single quotes, double quotes and backticks all make text. Pick one and stick with it.

stages.l:
You did it! That's a real program. Now make it yours. Whatever is between the quotes gets printed, so you can say anything.

console.log("I am going to make a game!");
stages.p: Change the starter so it prints a message of your own, anything except Hello, world!. One line or a few, it's up to you.
stages.h: Replace the words between the quotes with your own, like console.log("Robin was here");
alts:
console.log("Robin was here");
console.log("Coding is fun!");
stages.altNote: Any message counts, and you can print as many lines as you like.

stages.l:
A program runs from top to bottom, one line at a time. Each console.log prints on its own line.

console.log("Player 1");
console.log("Player 2");
Player 1
Player 2
stages.p: Print three lines, in this order: Ready, then Set, then Go!
stages.h: Three console.log lines, one under the other. The first is console.log("Ready");
stages.st: // Print Ready, Set, Go! on three lines
stages.altNote: Inside text, \n means "start a new line", so one console.log can print all three lines.

stages.reqMsg: For the second line, let JavaScript do the math: write 2 + 2 without quotes, for example console.log(2 + 2);
stages.l:
Quotes tell JavaScript "this is text, print it exactly". Numbers don't need quotes, and without quotes JavaScript does the math for you.

console.log("10 + 5");
console.log(10 + 5);
10 + 5
15

Text in quotes is called a string. A plain number is a number.
stages.p: Print the text 2 + 2 on the first line, then let JavaScript work out 2 + 2 on the second line.
stages.h: Text in quotes is printed exactly as written; without quotes JavaScript calculates it. Use one console.log of each kind.
stages.st:
// line 1: the text 2 + 2
// line 2: the answer

stages.reqMsg: Keep the Shield line, but turn it into a comment: put // in front of it (or wrap it in /* and */).
stages.l:
Any line that starts with // is a comment. JavaScript skips it completely. Comments are notes for humans, and they're handy for switching a line off without deleting it.

// This is a note. It doesn't run.
console.log("Hi");
// console.log("This line is switched off");
Hi

You've already seen comments in the starter code. Now you know what they are!
stages.p: The starter prints three items. Turn the Shield line into a comment so only Sword and Bow print. Don't delete it: a comment keeps the line around for later.
stages.h: Put // at the very start of the middle line.
stages.altNote: /* ... */ is a block comment. It can hide one line or many.

stages.l:
Here's a secret: every programmer sees errors all the time. An error just means JavaScript got confused by something you typed. It's not a disaster, it's a clue.

When your code has an error, press RUN anyway. The game shows the message and explains it in plain words, usually with the line number. A very common one is a missing quote: text has to start and end with ".

console.log("Oops);    // broken: no closing quote
console.log("Oops");   // fixed
stages.p: The starter has a mistake. Press RUN to see the error, then fix it so it prints Level up!
stages.h: The text starts with a quote but never ends with one. Add " right after the !
stages.altNote: Any matching pair of quotes fixes it. The start and end quote just have to be the same kind.

stages.l:
A variable is a labelled box that holds a value. You make one with let, a name, =, and the value.

let lives = 3;

Read it as "let lives be 3". From now on, the name lives means 3.
stages.p: Make a variable called coins that holds the number 5.
stages.h: Use let, then the name, then = and the value, like let lives = 3;.
stages.altNote: const works too, for values that never change. And the value can be worked out, as long as it ends up as 5.

stages.reqMsg: Print the variable itself: console.log(hero); with no quotes around hero.
stages.l:
To see what's inside a variable, print its name without quotes. With quotes you'd just print the word itself.

let lives = 3;
console.log(lives);
console.log("lives");
3
lives
stages.p: The starter makes a variable hero. Print what's inside it.
stages.h: Put the variable name inside the brackets of console.log( ), with no quotes.

stages.reqMsg: Change hp using hp itself, so it works whatever hp was before: hp = hp - 3; (or hp -= 3;)
stages.l:
Variables can change. That's why they're called variables! Use = again, but without let this time, because the box already exists.

let lives = 3;
lives = lives - 1;   // now 2

lives = lives - 1 means "work out lives minus 1, then put that back into lives".
stages.p: Your hero has 10 hp and gets hit for 3 damage. Subtract 3 from hp.
stages.h: Set hp to itself minus the damage, like score = score + 1; adds one.
stages.altNote: hp -= 3 is a shortcut for hp = hp - 3. A damage variable makes it easy to change later.

stages.reqMsg: Use the variables in your math, for example coins * 2.
stages.l:
JavaScript is a great calculator. These are the math symbols:

SymbolMeaningExample
+add4 + 2 is 6
-subtract4 - 2 is 2
*multiply4 * 2 is 8
/divide4 / 2 is 2

You can do math with variables too:

let lives = 3;
console.log(lives + 1);
4
stages.p: Using the variables, print coins doubled, then print coins minus price.
stages.h: Use * to multiply and - to subtract, with one console.log for each result.
stages.banMsg: Let JavaScript work the answers out from coins and price instead of typing 24 and 7.

stages.reqMsg: Build the message from the name variable, with + (or a template literal), not by typing Robin.
stages.l:
With text, + joins pieces together, end to end.

let item = "potion";
console.log("You found a " + item + "!");
console.log("Coins: " + 12);
You found a potion!
Coins: 12
Tip

Spaces matter. Put the space inside the quotes, like "You found a ", or the words will be squashed together.
stages.p:
Use + and the name variable to print Hello, Robin!

Already know template literals (the `...${ }` kind)? Those count too.
stages.h: Join strings and variables with +, like "Bye, " + friend. Remember the comma, the space and the !.
stages.st:
let name = "Robin";
// print Hello, Robin! using name

stages.reqMsg: Use an if to decide whether to print, so it only happens when hp is 0 or less.
stages.l:
if lets your program make a choice. The code inside the curly braces { } only runs when the check in the brackets is true.

let coins = 20;
if (coins >= 10) {
  console.log("You can buy a sword");
}
You can buy a sword

Some handy checks: > more than, < less than, >= at least, <= at most, === exactly equal.
stages.p: Print Game over, but only if hp is 0 or less.
stages.h: Use an if with the <= operator to check hp, and put the console.log inside its braces.
stages.st:
let hp = 0;
// if hp is 0 or less, print Game over
stages.altNote: hp < 1 means the same as hp <= 0 for whole numbers. For a one-line if, the braces are optional (but they help when you add more lines).

stages.reqMsg: Use a loop for this one (a for loop is the classic way), instead of three console.log lines.
stages.l:
A for loop repeats code for you. This one counts with a variable i:

for (let i = 1; i <= 5; i++) {
  console.log("Round " + i);
}

It has three parts, split by ;

  • let i = 1: start at 1
  • i <= 5: keep going while i is 5 or less
  • i++: add 1 to i after each round
stages.p: Use a for loop to print 1, 2 and 3, each on its own line.
stages.h: Use the same loop, but keep going only while i <= 3, and print just i.
stages.st: // count from 1 to 3 with a for loop
stages.altNote: A while loop works too, and so does counting from 0 and printing i + 1.

stages.l:
A function is a named recipe you can use again and again. You give it inputs, and return hands back an answer.

function double(n) {
  return n * 2;
}
console.log(double(4));
console.log(double(10));
8
20

n is the input. Each time you call double(...), n is whatever you put in the brackets.
stages.p: Finish greet(name) so it returns "Hi, ", then the name, then "!". For example greet("Robin") returns "Hi, Robin!".
stages.h: Join the pieces with + and return them, like return "Bye, " + who; but with the "!" on the end.
stages.altNote: A template literal or an arrow function gives the same result. You'll meet arrows properly later.

stages.reqMsg: Work out the next level with math from the level variable, like level + 1.
stages.banMsg: Use the name and job variables instead of typing Robin or Mage into the console.log lines.
stages.l:
Time to put it all together: variables, joining text with +, and a little math. Once this card prints, you've finished the tutorial. Amazing work!

Next stop: the Main Path. Start with Variables and keep going from there. You already know more than you think.
stages.p:
Use the variables to print this card exactly:

== Intro card ==
Name: Robin
Class: Mage
Level: 3
Next level: 4
stages.h: The second line is console.log("Name: " + name); For the last line, put the math in brackets: "Next level: " + (level + 1)
